findings.issue: Defense-in-depth gap on token-as-path-segment. The token is interpolated into the URI template `/bot{token}/...` while the WebClient is configured with `DefaultUriBuilderFactory.EncodingMode.NONE` (line 51). With NONE-encoding, reserved URI characters in the substituted variable (`/`, `?`, `#`, `..`) are NOT percent-encoded and pass through verbatim into the request path. A token containing `/` or `?` would let an attacker pivot the request to a different Telegram method (e.g. `0:secret/sendMessage?chat_id=X&text=Y` would hit `sendMessage` instead of `getMe` if such a string ever reached the client). The current upstream defense is a single `@Pattern` bean-validation on `ConnectBotRequest.token` (D16) which forbids those characters by the bot-token regex shape. However, `TelegramApiClient` is now a reusable @Component — every future caller (BotService task 4, webhook ingestion 06b, sender 06c, internal jobs, tests, scheduled re-validation) must remember to validate the token before calling. There is no defense-in-depth at the client layer.
findings.suggestion: Either (a) drop `EncodingMode.NONE` and rely on the default `TEMPLATE_AND_VALUES` which percent-encodes the variable (test that Telegram still accepts the encoded token — they do, the token is `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+` per Telegram contract and is unchanged under percent-encoding), OR (b) add a single guard at the top of each public method: `if (token == null || !TOKEN_SHAPE.matcher(token).matches()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid token shape");` with `private static final Pattern TOKEN_SHAPE = Pattern.compile("\\d{1,20}:[A-Za-z0-9_-]{30,50}");` — the same regex already used by the scrubber. Option (b) keeps the URI template explicit and adds the defense at the trust boundary where the value enters the client.

findings.where: backend/src/main/java/com/botfunnel/bot/TelegramApiClient.java (no global log filter); also reactor / WebClient default behavior
findings.issue: The token-regex scrubber on line 142-145 is applied ONLY to strings the client itself feeds into `log.warn` via `toAppException` (line 109). It is NOT a Logback-level converter / turbo-filter / appender filter and therefore does not protect against three real leak vectors that exist even without our own code emitting a token: (1) Spring's `WebClientResponseException` for 5xx responses carries a default message of the shape `"503 Service Unavailable from GET https://api.telegram.org/bot<TOKEN>/getMe"` (full URI including token). On retry the exception flows through `Retry.backoff` — at default log levels nothing logs it, but if anyone raises `logging.level.org.springframework.web.reactive.function.client=DEBUG` or `logging.level.reactor.util.retry=DEBUG` (a common debugging move), every retry attempt logs the URI with the token. (2) Reactor Netty wiretap or `logging.level.reactor.netty.http.client=DEBUG` logs the request URI for every call, again token in path. (3) If any future caller catches the eventual error and does `log.error("bot call failed", ex)` (the natural reflex), the stack trace's message of the original WCRE is in the cause chain. R1 / AC17 set a hard bar ("no log line carries it") and the current implementation depends on operators never turning up reactive log levels — fragile.
findings.owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures (sensitive data in logs)
findings.suggestion: Add a Logback `MessageConverter` or pattern-layout converter that runs `scrubTokens` over every emitted message, registered via `logback-spring.xml`, so the protection is policy-level rather than call-site-level. Example: implement `com.botfunnel.bot.log.TokenScrubbingConverter extends ClassicConverter` whose `convert(ILoggingEvent)` returns `scrubTokens(event.getFormattedMessage())` and reference it in the encoder pattern. Alternatively, change line 60 to use a path that does NOT inline the token in a URI segment — Telegram requires the token in the path, but you can wire it as a header/param if you proxy through your own intermediate — out of scope for this task. At minimum, document in the module README that `logging.level.reactor=DEBUG` and `logging.level.org.springframework.web.reactive.function.client=DEBUG` MUST NOT be enabled in any environment, and add a startup check that warns if those levels are set. Task scope is the client itself, so the Logback converter is the right unit of work.

findings.issue: `mapClientError` uses `HttpStatus.resolve(...)` which returns `null` for any status code that is not in the `HttpStatus` enum (e.g. a non-standard 4xx code like 418 is fine, but exotic upstream codes like 499 — used by some CDNs — resolve to null). When `status == null`, line 108's guard `status != null && status.is4xxClientError()` is false, so the code falls through to line 115 (`AppException.badRequest(scrubbed == null ? "Telegram client error" : scrubbed)`) and the scrubbed-but-otherwise-raw Telegram `description` becomes the AppException message. `GlobalErrorHandler.handleAppException` returns `ex.getMessage()` to the user (`/Users/pavlokorolov/IdeaProjects/simple-sender/backend/src/main/java/com/botfunnel/common/GlobalErrorHandler.java:23`). The scrubber removes the token shape but does NOT remove other things Telegram might quote back: a webhook secret (if Telegram echoes it), an internal IP, a verbose stack-shape string. R1 / AC17 specifically protect the token; this is a narrower information-disclosure concern about everything else in `description`.
findings.owasp: A04:2021 Insecure Design (information disclosure via verbatim upstream error)
findings.suggestion: Drop the `description` from the user-facing message on the fallback branch. Replace line 115 with `return AppException.badRequest("Telegram client error");` (always generic). The scrubbed description still gets logged at WARN on line 109 inside the `is4xxClientError` branch, so operators see it; the fallback branch never reaches that log because its guard is mutually exclusive — add a symmetric `log.warn("Telegram client error (unrecognized status {}): {}", response.statusCode().value(), scrubbed);` before returning to keep operator visibility. This brings the fallback in line with the D8 principle (precise reason in logs, generic message to user).

findings.issue: The `isTransient` cause-chain walker on line 128-140 guards against a self-cause loop (`if (next == cur) break;` on line 136) but does not guard against a longer cycle (A -> B -> A). In practice, `Throwable.initCause` rejects `t.initCause(t)` (self-cause) but does NOT prevent longer cycles being constructed via the protected `Throwable(String, Throwable)` constructor or via `setStackTrace` shenanigans, and JLS does not forbid the JVM seeing a non-self cycle. With a 2-cycle, this walker becomes an infinite loop and pins a Reactor thread. Practically this is hard to trigger (Telegram and Spring don't construct such cycles), so risk is low — but a 16-iteration cap is a one-line hardening.
findings.owasp: A04:2021 Insecure Design (DoS via untrusted exception chain)
findings.suggestion: Add a depth cap: `int hops = 0; while (cur != null && hops++ < 16) { ... }` — cheap, future-proof, and the cap is well above any realistic exception nesting depth.

findings.issue: Token regex `\d{1,20}:[A-Za-z0-9_-]{30,50}` has no boundary anchors. Two minor consequences: (a) Substrings that happen to look like a token (random log noise) get redacted — false positives are operationally fine but slightly noisy. (b) More importantly, the lower bound `{30,50}` is loose; a future Telegram-format change pushing the secret to 51+ chars would mean tokens silently stop being redacted. Currently Telegram tokens have a 35-char secret per the user-spec line 279 wording, so 30-50 is a safe envelope, but it is wider than necessary on both ends and the test corpus (TelegramApiClientTest.java:27) uses exactly the canonical 35-char form so does not exercise the boundaries.
findings.owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures (incomplete redaction coverage)
findings.suggestion: Add a parameterized boundary test in `TelegramApiClientTest`: feed a 29-char-secret string (must NOT match), a 30-char (must match), a 50-char (must match), a 51-char (must NOT match — flags regression if Telegram widens the secret). Optionally tighten to `\d{8,12}:[A-Za-z0-9_-]{35}` to match the real Telegram contract, but the looser form has a reason (forward compat). Either way, lock the behavior with explicit boundary tests.

findings.issue: `setWebhook(token, url, secret)` accepts an arbitrary `url` and forwards it to Telegram with no validation that it is HTTPS, that it points to a domain owned by the platform, or that it is not a private/loopback address. As you note in the task brief, the open-redirect / SSRF surface here belongs to the caller (BotService task 4 will construct the URL from `${app.url}` + project id, controlled), so for THIS task the client behaves correctly. Confirming it explicitly: the client trusts its caller. The risk is that the client is now a reusable @Component, and any future caller (06b webhook re-arm, 06c sender, a test fixture, an ops script) that lets the URL be influenced by user input would inject an attacker-controlled webhook URL — Telegram would then POST update payloads (including bot-message text) to attacker infrastructure.
findings.suggestion: Out of scope for task 2 — confirmed. For the feature: add a guard in `BotService` (task 4) that the constructed webhook URL starts with the configured `${app.url}` (an exact prefix match), and reject anything else. Worth a one-line comment in `setWebhook`'s Javadoc: `// Caller is responsible for ensuring `url` is platform-controlled — do not pass user-provided URLs.`
